title: CTO and head of engineering situations
authored: Project-authored reflective scenarios (2026-10-23). Not a validated situational judgment test; there are no correct answers.

scenarios.title: Platform or product
scenarios.prompt: Product teams keep rebuilding the same infrastructure. Building a platform team would slow product delivery for two quarters.

options.text: Create the platform team now; the duplication will only grow.
Let one product team build shared components as they go.
Measure the duplication cost first, then decide.
Keep teams autonomous; duplication is the price of speed.

scenarios.title: Vendor lock-in
scenarios.prompt: A cloud provider offers a large discount for committing to its proprietary database for three years.

options.text: Take the deal; the savings are certain and migration is hypothetical.
Decline; portability is worth more than the discount.
Accept with an abstraction layer that keeps an exit path.
Model exit costs with finance before deciding.

scenarios.title: Security incident disclosure
scenarios.prompt: Your team finds evidence that an attacker accessed a database with customer emails. The investigation is incomplete.

options.text: Inform leadership, legal and affected customers as early as possible.
Finish the investigation to know the scope before telling anyone outside.
Let legal decide the timing; you focus on containment.
Brief the board immediately and follow their lead on disclosure.

scenarios.title: Cut costs by 20 percent
scenarios.prompt: The board asks engineering to cut costs by 20 percent within two quarters.

options.text: Cut infrastructure spend aggressively before touching headcount.
Ask each team lead to propose savings, then decide together.
Push back with the impact on the roadmap and negotiate the target.
Stop the lowest-value projects outright and reassign people.

scenarios.title: Hiring a VP of Engineering
scenarios.prompt: Your top VP candidate is brilliant but has a reputation for being hard on teams. The runner-up is steady and well liked.

options.text: Hire the brilliant candidate and coach them closely.
Hire the steady candidate; culture is harder to fix than skills.
Do deep back-channel references on the top candidate first.
Let senior engineers meet both candidates and weigh in.

scenarios.title: CEO demand versus tech strategy
scenarios.prompt: The CEO promises a customer an integration your architecture cannot support without a significant shortcut.

options.text: Tell the CEO plainly what the shortcut costs and propose an alternative.
Deliver the shortcut and plan the clean-up afterwards.
Meet the customer with the CEO to reshape the request.
Ask your architects to find a creative path before responding.

scenarios.title: Public outage
scenarios.prompt: A major outage lasts four hours and trends on social media. Customers want answers.

options.text: Publish a candid public postmortem within days, including what you got wrong.
Send a short apology now and a fuller report when the analysis is complete.
Let communications handle the public message; you focus on the fix.
Communicate privately with key customers and keep public statements minimal.

scenarios.title: Acquisition due diligence
scenarios.prompt: You have two weeks to assess the technology of a company your firm wants to acquire. Leadership is enthusiastic.

options.text: Run a structured review and report risks bluntly, even if it cools the deal.
Focus on the few areas most likely to hide serious problems.
Bring in an external firm to do the assessment.
Flag only deal-breakers; the rest can be fixed after the acquisition.

scenarios.title: AI adoption policy
scenarios.prompt: Engineers are already using various AI assistants without an agreed policy. Legal is nervous.

options.text: Publish a clear policy quickly with approved tools and data rules.
Pause all use until legal and security finish their review.
Form a working group of engineers and legal to draft the policy.
Encourage use and ask teams to share good practices informally.

scenarios.title: Multi-year migration
scenarios.prompt: Moving from a monolith to services is planned to take three years. After one year, progress is half of what was expected.

options.text: Re-plan honestly, communicate the new timeline and cut scope.
Add people and push harder to recover the schedule.
Question whether the migration is still worth finishing at all.
Keep going; large migrations are always slow at first.

scenarios.title: Culture problem
scenarios.prompt: An engagement survey shows engineers feel blamed for failures and afraid to take risks.

options.text: Address it in an all-hands, own your part, and commit to blameless reviews.
Ask managers to run listening sessions and report back.
Change specific processes, such as incident reviews, without a big announcement.
Bring in an external coach to work with leadership.

scenarios.title: Open-source licence risk
scenarios.prompt: A core product depends on a library that has just changed to a restrictive licence.

options.text: Start replacing it immediately, even if it delays features.
Pin the last permissive version and plan a replacement over time.
Ask legal for a full assessment before doing anything.
Negotiate a commercial licence with the maintainers.
